messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Known People: Related people, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Singh is a 49-year-old military medic who came to treatment after months of insisting to himself that he should be able to handle this on his own. The abuse had taken place inside his marriage, usually behind closed doors and most often at night, when arguments escalated and his wife pinned him with a force that still stunned him to remember. What remained most vividly were not complete stories but sensory fragments: the smell of sweat at close range, the sound of ordinary movement in the house turning sharp, the physical shock of being struck and held down by someone he knew intimately. He has great difficulty describing the episodes in a linear way. When he tries, he stalls, says there are “pieces” and “body memories,” and falls silent. Yet when something brings it back, he feels pain in the same parts of his body that were hurt at the time, and for a few moments he is not remembering so much as reliving it.

In the weeks after one particularly violent incident, Ravi found that certain cues could overturn him without warning. The smell of body odor in a cramped supply room at work, seeing police near the base entrance, or even encountering relatives connected to his wife could bring on the sense that the abuse was happening again. Those moments were not just reminders; they seemed to strip away time. He would feel the old pain return to his ribs and shoulders and become flooded with the certainty that he was back in that room. Because those triggers pulled him straight into reliving, he began to organize his life around avoiding them where he could. He stopped wearing clothes that resembled what he had worn during the assaults, withdrew from people who might ask about his marriage or connect him to her family, and gave up exercise, partly because sweat on his own body had become unbearable and partly because the bodily strain seemed to summon the same pain and helplessness.

What frightened Ravi almost as much as the memories was what they seemed to say about him. Each time he was thrown back into the event by a smell, a familiar face, or the sight of police, he was left with the thought that something was fundamentally wrong with him: a military medic who could respond under pressure for others, but not protect himself in his own home. The fact that no one had faced consequences deepened that conclusion. Seeing authority figures was especially poisonous; police did not register as safety, but as a reminder that nothing had happened, nobody had been held accountable, and he had somehow become the kind of man this could happen to. After these moments, life would feel stripped of purpose. He described going through shifts mechanically, unable to connect with the meaning he used to feel in caring for injured service members.

Those beliefs began to shape his days as much as the triggers did. Ravi had come to believe that because there was something defective in him, keeping to himself was the least humiliating option. He avoided other people at work when he could, took breaks alone, and stopped joining the physical training he once completed automatically with colleagues. The fewer places he went, the fewer people he saw, and soon only a very limited set of spaces felt safe—his office with the door closed, his car, one corner of the house. This shrinking of his world fed his sense that his life no longer meant much, and that retreat itself became another piece of evidence, in his mind, that he was no longer the man he had been.

At night the picture tightened further. Ravi lay awake because sleep felt like letting his guard down. He said he needed to stay alert, listening for ordinary sounds in the house, and he startled violently to noises that would not have bothered him before. In that keyed-up state, small cues became easier to detect and harder to dismiss: a faint smell, footsteps outside, a police cruiser glimpsed on the road the next morning. Hyperalertness seemed to prime the memories, and the reliving in turn confirmed for him that danger was still close. When he woke aching from a flash of memory or felt pain bloom in his body after a noise in the night, he took that as proof that he was damaged and permanently changed.

His avoidance, meant to contain all this, had begun to worsen it. By refusing exercise, he lost one of the few routines that had once grounded him. By avoiding people, he had fewer interruptions to the mental replay and fewer chances to test whether all familiar others were dangerous. By limiting himself to “safe” places, everything outside them felt increasingly charged, so that triggers appeared to multiply. He noticed he was scanning more, sleeping less, and feeling more easily ambushed by sensory fragments he still could not put into words. He finally sought help after nearly jumping at a routine sound in the clinic and then locking himself in a supply room when a coworker came in smelling strongly of sweat. What he fears most is that this is all his life is now: vigilance, shrinking, and shame. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is to stop feeling as if the abuse is still happening every time the world brushes against one of its traces.
